title: The First Amendment Clause That Stopped Doing Any Work
hook: The First Amendment names speech and the press separately — but the Court has folded the press clause into the speech clause, leaving journalists no rights an ordinary blogger lacks.
key_points: The First Amendment names the press separately from speech, implying the framers meant it to add something.
The Court has mostly declined to read it that way: the press gets the same protection as any other speaker, no more.
Branzburg v. Hayes (1972) found no First Amendment right for reporters to shield confidential sources.
Zurcher v. Stanford Daily (1978) allowed police to search a newsroom on a valid warrant; Pell v. Procunier (1974) denied special press access to prisons.
The press did win against discriminatory taxes — Grosjean (1936) and Minneapolis Star (1983) struck down levies aimed at publications.
SCOTUSblog notes references to "the press" in Court opinions collapsed from roughly 1,500 in the early 1970s to under 100 in the late 2010s.
content_html: The First Amendment protects "the freedom of speech, or of the press" — two phrases, joined by "or," which suggests the press was meant to get something speech alone doesn't. Writing at SCOTUSblog in August 2026, Eli Kronenberg argues the Supreme Court has quietly declined that reading. Journalists today are protected as speakers, not as the press; as First Amendment lawyer Floyd Abrams puts it in the piece, the press and every other speaker "are in exactly the same boat."
extra_html:
The pattern shows up across the Court's cases. Branzburg v. Hayes (1972) held reporters have no First Amendment privilege to refuse a grand jury's questions about confidential sources. Pell v. Procunier (1974) found no special press right of access to prisons. Zurcher v. Stanford Daily (1978) let police search a student newspaper's office on an ordinary warrant. The clear wins — Grosjean v. American Press Co. (1936) and Minneapolis Star v. Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue (1983) — were about taxes singling out publications, a kind of discrimination the speech clause would likely catch anyway.

Kronenberg cites a striking measure of the drift: mentions of "the press" in Supreme Court opinions fell from roughly 1,500 in the early 1970s to under 100 in the late 2010s. The Floyd Abrams Institute's new Press Clause Project is trying to give the clause work to do again, with proposals as concrete as reserved courtroom seating for reporters and protection from being dispersed from public events. Read the full piece at SCOTUSblog for the argument in the author's own terms.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

related.title: Can the Government Force a Reporter to Reveal a Source?
related.hook: There's no absolute First Amendment shield protecting a journalist's sources — which is exactly what makes a federal subpoena for reporters' grand jury testimony such a live threat to the free press.

related.title: Freedom of Expression
related.hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

prereqs.title: The Free Press & Democracy
prereqs.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean to say the First Amendment's press clause has become "invisible"?
flashcards.back_html: Courts protect journalists only as ordinary speakers under the speech clause, so the separate mention of "the press" adds no distinct right of its own.

flashcards.prompt: Which kind of press claim has actually succeeded at the Supreme Court?

choices.text: Challenges to taxes singling out publications, as in Grosjean and Minneapolis Star
Claims to a right to withhold confidential sources from a grand jury
Claims to a right of special access to prisons and inmates

flashcards.explanation_html: The Court struck down discriminatory press taxes, but rejected source protection in Branzburg and special access in Pell.

flashcards.prompt: In Zurcher v. Stanford Daily (1978), what did the Court permit?

choices.text: Police searching a newsroom under a valid warrant
Jailing an editor for refusing to name a source
A state tax on newsprint aimed at large papers

flashcards.explanation_html: Zurcher held a newsroom gets no extra shield against an otherwise valid search warrant.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a weak press clause matter even if the speech clause is strong?
flashcards.back_html: Newsgathering — protecting sources, getting access, resisting searches — is work ordinary speech protection doesn't cover, so the press has no tool tailored to it.
